cim: Scholars consider how to use AI in education without sacrificing learning

cim_eredeti: Scholars consider how to use AI in education without sacrificing learning
szoveg_eredeti:

Credit: Will Kirk / Johns Hopkins University

"Using artificial intelligence to do your homework is like taking a forklift to the gym," Jaime Young, a senior lecturer in chemistry at Johns Hopkins University, said he often tells students. "Sure, the weights are going to get lifted, but you are not getting stronger."

Young's analogy captures a central challenge facing educators: AI can help students complete an assignment, but does it help them learn? As the technology enters classrooms and reshapes expectations in the workplace, educators are seeking ways to use AI to deepen students' understanding without bypassing the thinking that builds it.

That challenge brought scholars, educators, and students together on Oct. 27 for the university's Data Science and AI Institute Fall 2026 Symposium, Artificial Intelligence and Human Learning. The event explored how AI could strengthen learning, how commercial interests could undermine that promise, and how students can develop judgment and purpose in a world increasingly shaped by the technology.

"We don't want AI to take the place of learning for the student," said Mark Dredze, DSAI's director and a computer science professor at Johns Hopkins, in his opening remarks. "We want AI to help enable the student to learn."

Doing so requires research into how AI affects students' understanding and the design of tools that "ask useful questions, expose misconceptions, and help learners evaluate their own reasoning," he said.

In the keynote address, Munther Dahleh, founding director of the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, emphasized the need for ethical design and transparency in AI systems and digital platforms, including those used for shopping, navigation, and social media. Companies that run such systems, he said, often use data to advance their own interests, with complex algorithms feeding users only partial views of the information available—and influencing the opinions users form and actions they take.

Image credit: Will Kirk / Johns Hopkins University

"With generative AI and the ability to do computation at scale, data becomes the most important thing that we have," Dahleh said. "Platforms are trying to persuade you to do something. They need your private information to do that."

Dahleh also raised questions about whether AI helps people make informed judgments or gives companies greater power over those judgments. In a panel discussion that followed, moderator Sri Sarma, a professor in the Department of Biomedical Engineering at Johns Hopkins, asked panelists whether influence is "always bad." Public health campaigns, educational interventions, and energy conservation programs also seek to change behavior, she noted.

"If AI can influence people more effectively, why shouldn't we use it to promote better outcomes?" Sarma asked.

The answer depends on who defines those outcomes, said Debra Mathews, associate director for research and programs at the Johns Hopkins Berman Institute of Bioethics and a professor in the School of Medicine's Department of Genetic Medicine.

"I would frame the question as: Whose values are driving the development and deployment of these technologies?" Mathews said. "It's not our collective values that are driving these."

Government regulation and other measures, she said, are needed "to ensure that these technologies better serve both our collective and individual interests and values."

Competitive pressure can also drive people to adopt AI, despite concerns about its consequences, said Mario Macis, an economics professor at the Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. Macis mentioned a study by Leo Bursztyn and others from the University of Chicago.

Image credit: Will Kirk / Johns Hopkins University

"The study found that parents are more willing to pay for an AI tool to help their kids in school when they know other parents are making the same decision," Macis said. "Even though 80% of parents are worried about the potential long-term consequences of AI on learning," they decided to make that investment—and follow the herd mentality.

"Perhaps in this context, the market is not sufficient" to regulate itself, given that AI companies are unlikely to sacrifice their own gain for the benefit of society. "Maybe we need rules," Macis said.

As chief of artificial intelligence at Northeastern University in Boston, Javed (Jay) Aslam spearheads a program that integrates AI across the school's curriculum while preparing students for a job market deemed by his research to value one thing above all: AI readiness.

"Employers want orchestrators, not passive operators, of AI," Aslam said. "They're really demanding it."

Northeastern's three-tiered AI curriculum starts with fundamental concepts to help students become fluent so they can apply what they've learned to a specific discipline. Then comes agency, the most sought-after capability, which includes being able to teach AI skills to coworkers.

Through a partnership with Microsoft, Northeastern created an AI makerspace on campus, mostly run by students.

"It's almost like an Apple Genius Bar, where you can walk in and say, 'Hey, I want to build an AI agent to do X, Y, or Z, or I want to build a personalized tutor for my class … or a virtual 24/7 teaching assistant for the course I'm teaching, or … improve this operational workflow,'" Aslam said. "And there will be people who can help you do it on the spot."

Young, the senior lecturer in chemistry at JHU's Krieger School of Arts and Sciences, said AI can help students get more practice with challenging material. His students often use the tools as tutors, generating additional practice problems and troubleshooting gaps in their understanding. The practice appears to pay off, with his exam scores surpassing those from previous years, he said.

Illysa Izenberg, an associate teaching professor at the Center for Leadership Education in the university's Whiting School of Engineering, said she encourages students to consider how AI aligns with their reasons for getting an education in the first place. She asks them to reflect on what they came to Johns Hopkins to learn and what they hope to gain from the experience, while acknowledging the pressures they face.

Image caption: AI in the Classroom panelists Illysa Izenberg, David Dowdy, and Brian Klaas

Image credit: Will Kirk / Johns Hopkins University

"I recognize they're overloaded," Izenberg said. "They're in a hurry. They feel they need the As—these are the headwinds we're always going to push against."

When Izenberg permits AI on an assignment, she explains how using it can support the learning goals and requires students to reflect on and write about their experience. When she prohibits it, she explains how using it would undermine those goals. "I have a total AI transparency policy in my class," Izenberg continued. "I set a sort of contract between us at the start of the semester, promising that I will be transparent with them when I use it … and [saying] I expect the same from them."

The process takes time, she added, but it keeps the focus on student learning.

Douglas Knecht, senior director of Education Practice and Innovation at the University of Southern California's Center for Affective Neuroscience, Development, Learning and Education, or USC CANDLE, questioned the incentives for students' use of AI among adolescents, using a definition that spans ages 12 to 25 and encompasses continuing brain maturation.

He argued that when students care more about outcomes—finishing their work, their GPAs, and college and job acceptances—than they do about truly learning, it makes sense that they would use generative AI as a shortcut.
